newsitem.title: CANADA: Inco workers on strike, analysts ponder impact.
newsitem.headline: Inco workers on strike, analysts ponder impact.

text.p: Striking workers at Canadian nickel giant Inco Ltd.'s Sudbury, Ontario division walked picket lines on Tuesday, while analysts said a prolonged shutdown would be bullish for nickel prices.
Shares in Inco, the Western world's biggest nickel producer, rose on the Toronto Stock Exchange on Tuesday as news of the Sudbury strike sparked a brief rally on metal markets.
Company and union officials said they did not know when talks would resume.

"My current thinking is either this thing is settled in the next week or two, or it is likely to drift through July," Manford Mallory, an analyst with Research Capital Corp., said in a telephone interview.
Under normal operations, Sudbury produces more than 20 million pounds of nickel a month. London Metal Exchange (LME) inventories are estimated at 110 million pounds of nickel, Mallory said.
"It starts to eat into those LME inventories pretty quickly. If the strike lasts several weeks, it could start to have a meaningful pyschological impact," Mallory said.
Another analyst said: "If the strike were to go on for four or 4-1/2 months, you would get down to all-time record low (nickel inventory) levels."
According to Inco's 1997 production plan, the Ontario division was expected to produce about 230 million pounds of nickel, about 200 million pounds of copper and about four million pounds of cobalt.
Inco's 4,670 unionized Sudbury workers went on strike at midnight on Monday, after voting 60.4 percent against a tentative contract agreement reached last Friday.

Inco's Port Colborne, Ontario refinery, which processes cobalt, precious metals and electro-nickel, was not affected by the Sudbury strike. Unionized workers at the refinery approved the contract on Monday.
"At this point we're taking it on a day by day basis, but we have several weeks (supply) down there," Inco spokesman Jerry Rodgers said in a telephone interview.
Sudbury and Port Colborne were scheduled for a maintenance shutdown in early July.
Inco stock was up C10 cents to C$44.50 on the Toronto Stock Exchange in afternoon trading on Tuesday. It was up 12.5 cents to $32.375 on the New York Stock Exchange.
Analysts said Inco's stock would be more sensitive to nickel prices than the company's immediate production numbers. But that would depend on the length of the strike.
"In theory, a lot of what they would lose on volume they would gain on higher prices, but there's not much sign of prices staying higher," the second analyst said.

Asian buying pushed three-month nickel prices to a peak of $7,330 a tonne on news of the Sudbury strike. But prices later settled down to close at $7,180 per tonne after Russia's Norilsk said it may boost annual production by 20 percent.
Mallory said his earnings estimate for Inco was under review pending the outcome of the strike. Inco would likely absorb some costs related to the strike in its second-quarter results, he said.
"If it becomes a long strike it becomes a tougher tradeoff. How much does it move prices versus lost production?" he said.
